questions.prompt: In the relational model, what is the degree of a relation?

options.text: The number of attributes in the relation
The number of foreign keys referencing it
The number of tuples in the relation

questions.explanation: Degree (or arity) is the number of attributes, the width of the table. The number of tuples is the cardinality.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is TRUE about a candidate key?

options.text: It must always be a single attribute
A relation can have at most one candidate key
It may contain NULL values in the primary key column

questions.explanation: A candidate key is a superkey with no redundant attributes; removing any attribute destroys uniqueness. A relation may have several, and one is chosen as the primary key.

questions.prompt: The entity integrity constraint states that:

options.text: Every foreign key must match some primary key value
No attribute of a primary key may be NULL
Every relation must have at least one foreign key

questions.explanation: Entity integrity forbids NULLs in any primary key attribute, since a NULL would make the tuple unidentifiable. Matching foreign keys is referential integrity.

questions.prompt: In an ER diagram, a weak entity set is characterised by:

options.text: Having no primary key of its own, depending on an identifying owner
Being connected only to other weak entity sets

questions.explanation: A weak entity lacks a sufficient key of its own. It is identified by its partial key combined with the primary key of its identifying (owner) entity, via a total, identifying relationship.

questions.prompt: A relationship set R between entity sets A and B is many-to-one from A to B. This means:

options.text: Each entity in A associates with at most one entity in B
Each entity in B associates with at most one entity in A
Each entity in A associates with exactly one entity in B
Both A and B associate with many entities

questions.explanation: Many-to-one from A to B means many A entities may map to one B entity, so each A entity is related to at most one B entity. 'At most' rather than 'exactly' because participation may be partial.

questions.prompt: Which relational algebra operation requires the two operand relations to be union-compatible?
questions.explanation: Union, intersection and set difference all require union compatibility: the same degree and matching attribute domains. Cartesian product and join impose no such requirement.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the basic (primitive) operations of relational algebra?
questions.explanation: The primitive set is selection, projection, union, set difference, Cartesian product and rename. Natural join is derived: it can be expressed as a product followed by a selection and a projection.

questions.prompt: A foreign key in relation R referencing relation S may be NULL. What does this represent?

options.text: A tuple in R that participates in no relationship with S
An error that the DBMS must reject

questions.explanation: Referential integrity requires a foreign key to either match an existing primary key in S or be entirely NULL. A NULL simply means the tuple currently has no counterpart; partial participation.

questions.prompt: Which level of the three-schema architecture describes WHAT data is stored and the relationships among it, independent of physical storage?
questions.explanation: The conceptual level describes the whole database logically. The external level exposes per-user views, and the internal level describes physical storage. Separating them gives physical and logical data independence.

questions.prompt: If relation R has 5 tuples and relation S has 3 tuples, how many tuples are in R × S (Cartesian product)?
questions.explanation: The Cartesian product pairs every tuple of R with every tuple of S, giving 5 × 3 = 15 tuples. Its degree is the sum of the two degrees.
